title: Changing times, talking horns, reading music, and touring white bands
summary: He remembers white criticism of mutes, how horns 'talked', his advice to learn to read, and how white pit bands respected his section on tour.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: That was the number. And he got a little more ingenious because they told him he'd have to get out of it. But he died before he ever played anymore. And it wouldn't change his style for nothing. Well, I knew back in all the times that I was coming along that the time was changing. Well, up until 1918 they hadn't got a change yet. See, because still the white musicians were still criticizing the Negro musicians were playing music because they said that it never would last nowhere. That putting, they say, a beer bucket over a trumpet or something like that will never work. And every time they'd see me and I'd reach down and come in the place and I'd take my beer bucket or something and put it over there and come and say, womp, womp, womp, like that and make the horn talk like me and Freddie used to play because that's what we feel like doing, like whatever your name was. If we knew you, I could call your name on that mouthpiece just the same as I could out without saying anything. See? We talked on the horns. That's what I heard. That's right. Yeah. We played chicken reel and numbers like that. that boy, we played like the number goes, and you'd hear me say, and Bambi said, and I'd say, and then I'd say, and all those kind of things. So those were things that we had an idea that they had to catch off us to beat us playing. But as I come along, I told most of the boys, regardless of what you know, the freak that you can play on an instrument, learn how to read music. That's the greatest thing. And I'm so glad that I did since even I met my wife and the teachers that I went with, too, taught me how to read. And it helped me so that men like down in Chicago theater, those men down like that, when I went off, I didn't know how much my music went, met to me until I left here and went on the off-hand circuit and met them different white bands playing on the stand. We left here with fourteen pieces. And without a word of doubt, I wouldn't tell you a story, everywhere we'd go, and we'd open them first shows, and that white band would sit down on that pit at night and look at us like this. And when the show was off, they'd say, I want to meet your first trumpet player. And that's how I got my courage. It all come down. I met my greatest band, two of the greatest bands. One was in, uh, Pass, where's Dominic? Where did Dominic? Where did I tell you Dominic, the boy, cut Dominic's wrist about the girl?
